concepts.title: Central Tendency: The Idea of an Average

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Central Tendency: The Idea of an Average' refers to.
questions.a: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents a whole data set -- an average around which the observations cluster. The chapter presents the three classic measures: arithmetic mean, median and mode, each suited to different kinds of data and purposes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Central Tendency: The Idea of an Average'.
questions.a: One number to stand for many -- the average condenses a series into its centre.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Central Tendency: The Idea of an Average' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Calculate the arithmetic mean of the given observations. Use the method 'Arithmetic Mean: Simple and Weighted'. Work with: obs_count = 45, x1 = 12, x2 = 15, x3 = 240, x4 = 100, x5 = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.

Find the missing frequency given the mean of the series. Use the method 'Arithmetic Mean: Simple and Weighted'. Work with: obs_count = 15, x1 = 240, x2 = 300, x3 = 45, x4 = 15, x5 = 6. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mean.
Explain in your own words what 'Arithmetic Mean: Simple and Weighted' refers to.
questions.a: The arithmetic mean divides the sum of all observations by their number; for a frequency series, values are first multiplied by their frequencies. A weighted mean multiplies each value by an assigned importance before averaging, letting significance -- not just occurrence -- shape the result.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Arithmetic Mean: Simple and Weighted'.
questions.a: Sum over count -- the mean uses every observation, which is its strength and its sensitivity alike.

concepts.title: Median and Mode: Position and Frequency

questions.q: Using the method 'Median and Mode: Position and Frequency', work with: mid_high = 240, mid_low = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of median_even.
Take the relation taught for 'Median and Mode: Position and Frequency' and work with: mid_high = 25, mid_low = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of median_even.
Explain in your own words what 'Median and Mode: Position and Frequency' refers to.
questions.a: The median is the middle observation of an ordered series -- the value splitting the data in equal halves -- and for an even count it is the average of the two central values. The mode is the most frequently occurring value. Both resist extreme values, which distort the mean.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Median and Mode: Position and Frequency'.
questions.a: Median sits at the middle of the queue; mode is the crowd's favourite -- both laugh at extremes.
